chapter: Army service and after the war
title: GAC bookings, Clyde Bernhardt and 90 straight one-nighters
summary: He went into the Army in May 1944 after GAC booked solidly; trombonist Clyde Bernhardt joined and complained that 90 straight one-nighters was too much.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Oh, until I went in the Army.
So what would that be, the year that you were hooked by GMAC, then? Before you went in the Army, or was it longer than that?
It had to be longer.
What year did you go in the Army?
I went in the Army in 1944.
Oh, so then it was, wasn't it?
Uh-huh, yes. And -- yes, it was 1944, May, when I went in the service. But I do remember this. That GMAC had no trouble booking us, because Clyde Bernhardt, I guess you remember him, trombone player?
Yeah, yeah.
He was with the band then. He played with Louis Russell's band, and he came up with this other band that -- I don't know if it was the band that he came up the river with.
From where?
From New Orleans. He was one of the old timers, Clyde is, you know.
Oh, yes, yes.
And, anyway, -- I can't think of the
(Unintelligible.)
Wait a minute, wait a minute, maybe
I'm -- I don't want to get myself mixed, now. This would have to be after Fate [Marable]
Well, he's got a lot -- I know Clyde Bernhardt.
Who was the guy that brought Armstrong up the river?
Joe Glaser.
King Oliver.
King Oliver. He played with the King Oliver band.
Oh, yes, he did.

Yes, that's what I'm trying to get around to. Yes, Clyde played with King Oliver, you know. Because he used to tell me a lot of different things about when he was with King Oliver, and also when he was with Edgar Hayes and --
That was after Louis was with King Oliver. That was in the latter period.
Uh-huh, yes, that's true. So Clyde tickled me, though, because at one time we did -- I think it was 90 straight one-nighters.
How many?
90. And Clyde told me -- he came to me and says, McShann, I love to work and I have more fun with this band than I ever -- any band I have ever been with. And I enjoy

this band, but I'm going to have to take some time off, because you all work too much for me. He says, I got to take three weeks at least off. I'm going back to New York for three or four weeks, and I'll call you and I'll join you back if you ain't got nobody, if you got a place for me.
And that's what he did.
Were you making fairly good money when you were doing this?

Yes, I was making it, uh-huh. That Burl Adams -- well, it was just a matter -- he didn't have any trouble selling the group, because, see, the records was hot. But the other guys had something else in mind.
It was a setup.
Yes. See, they had had something else in mind, and that's just -- and we were lucky we came out like we did.
